name: Pentapeptide-3

card.summary: An ambiguous peptide name: historically KTTKS (Matrixyl), also tied to Vialox; little verified evidence.
card.note: The name referred to different peptides at different times; check the full ingredient name.

quick.overview:
Pentapeptide-3 is a cosmetic peptide label whose meaning has changed: before 2006 it denoted palmitoyl KTTKS (Matrixyl), and it is also tied to the Vialox brand.

Research is mostly laboratory work on KTTKS-type peptides, and no clinical trial specific to Vialox was found.
quick.mechanism: KTTKS-type peptides are described as matrikines that signal cells to make collagen and other matrix proteins; Vialox is described by suppliers as reducing muscle signalling, which this wiki could not verify.
quick.risks: No adverse events were reported in the sources. A cell study found KTTKS analogues non-cytotoxic to fibroblasts.

lead: Pentapeptide-3 is a cosmetic peptide ingredient used in topical anti-wrinkle products, where it is meant to smooth fine lines and give skin a firmer, younger-looking surface. The name is ambiguous: before 2006 the INCI name palmitoyl pentapeptide-3 referred to the Lys-Thr-Thr-Lys-Ser (KTTKS) peptide sold as Matrixyl, since renamed palmitoyl pentapeptide-4.[1][2] The ingredient sold as Vialox is also described as a pentapeptide and is marketed as a muscle-relaxing, expression-line-softening ingredient.[4]

The KTTKS family is described in the literature as matrikines, fragments of collagen that stimulate extracellular matrix production and type I and III collagen expression in cultured cells, which is the basis for their use in anti-wrinkle creams.[2][3] A 2019 study of KTTKS analogues found none cytotoxic to fibroblasts.[2]

A 2026 laboratory study evaluated Vialox and a second pentapeptide, Leuphasyl, with computer docking, molecular dynamics and a cell cytotoxicity assay. It reported that Vialox preferentially targeted SIRT-1 in the models and that neither peptide was cytotoxic to HaCaT skin cells at concentrations up to 1 mg/mL.[4]

chain: A peptide is applied in a cream or serum
It is described as signalling skin cells or relaxing muscle signalling
Fine lines and expression lines look softer
angle.text: Pentapeptide-3 products are used on the face, especially around the eyes and forehead, to soften the look of wrinkles. KTTKS-type peptides are described as prompting collagen production in cells, while Vialox is marketed as reducing muscle-driven expression lines; both are used as topical, cosmetic-counter alternatives to injections.

infobox: Palmitoyl pentapeptide-3 is the pre-2006 INCI name for KTTKS (now pentapeptide-4)[1][2]

paras: Palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (Matrixyl) is KTTKS joined to a 16-carbon palmitoyl chain, launched by Sederma around 2000.[1] It is a matrikine, a peptide fragment thought to signal cells to produce extracellular matrix, and a 2019 paper notes it was previously labelled palmitoyl pentapeptide-3.[2][3]

Vialox is a cosmeceutical pentapeptide used in anti-aging products. A 2026 study in Chemistry & Biodiversity describes it and Leuphasyl as potential noninvasive dermocosmetic agents and examines how they bind matrix metalloproteinases (which break down collagen) and Sirtuin-1 (a regulator of cellular ageing).[4] In that work Leuphasyl interacted more strongly with MMP-13, while Vialox preferentially targeted SIRT-1, and predictions suggested favourable pharmacokinetic and safety profiles.[4]

The 2019 KTTKS analogue study found none of the tested peptides cytotoxic to fibroblasts, and three promoted cell growth.[3] The 2026 Vialox work found no cytotoxicity on HaCaT cells up to 1 mg/mL.[4]

No studies found in people for a product specified as pentapeptide-3 or Vialox. Laboratory studies of KTTKS peptides show collagen-related effects in cells; the 2019 study found palmitoylated analogues inhibited serine proteases such as plasmin and thrombin in the laboratory and did not reproduce a previously reported 150 percent collagen increase.[2][3] The 2026 Vialox work used computer modelling and a cell cytotoxicity assay.[4]

timeline.event: Palmitoyl pentapeptide-3 is renamed palmitoyl pentapeptide-4.[2]
A study of 32 KTTKS analogues finds them non-cytotoxic to fibroblasts.[2][3]
First combined computational and cell study of Vialox and Leuphasyl published.[4]
